Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Internal factors for cyber sickness are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness, including age, gender, motion sickness (MS) susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.

Body awareness, the ability of the user to attend to and perceive bodily sensations, is a physical condition related to cyber sickness; poor sleep quality can affect this awareness and may contribute to or increase the severity of cyber sickness.
Latency in virtual reality (VR) is the time delay, or time gap, between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.
Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.

Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Means of locomotion, meaning how a user moves in a virtual world, is a content-related factor in cybersickness (CS), because a sensory mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause discomfort and disorientation that lead to cybersickness.

Visual complexity is an external factor that is positively correlated with cybersickness (CS) symptoms, so scenes with more objects of different shapes, sizes, and movements are more likely to induce cybersickness.

Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS).

The two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of three-dimensional (3D) space.
Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.
Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

Indirect manipulation is a method sometimes used to manipulate virtual objects in which the user does not directly manipulate the virtual object using the physical hand, but instead manipulates other objects mapped to the virtual object, and those other objects in turn manipulate the virtual object.

Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object.

Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

World in miniature (WIM) is a type of indirect proxy that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, which represents all objects in the virtual world, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding actual object in the virtual world.

A bimanual manipulation technique manipulates objects with both hands, and its hand movement can be synchronous, in which both hands move together, or asynchronous, in which the hands do not need to move simultaneously.

The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle.

Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric but synchronous technique and an extension of the spindle technique, in which both hands need to be moved together but need not be symmetrically placed around the sides of an imaginary axis.

Integrated hybrid manipulation techniques are techniques that switch automatically from selection to manipulation after selection, without any explicit signal from the user, and switch back to selection mode after manipulation.

Locomotion techniques, alternatively travel techniques, are techniques employed to let a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and to perceive that travel has taken place.
The travel part of navigation, also called locomotion, is the motor component of navigation and refers to the actual movement between two locations.
Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

Travel in navigation can be done by exploration, search, or maneuvering: exploration has no explicit goal or target point and the user moves around to see, learn, or explore; search is moving to a specified target location; and maneuvering comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination.

Selection-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user selects where to go rather than continuously specifying how to move there by steering or looking.

Travel in navigation can be accomplished using four broad types of locomotion techniques: walking-based locomotion, steering-based locomotion, selection-based locomotion, and manipulation-based locomotion.

Steering-based navigation has two types: spatial steering-based navigation, which is controlled using the user's body parts, and physical steering-based navigation, which is controlled using vehicular props or additional hardware.

Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

The objective of environment design is to make it easier for the user to build a mental map; if the design does not support creation of this mental map, many problems may occur and the overall user experience deteriorates.

The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model.

For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively.

Path following support for wayfinding can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.

Breadcrumb support for wayfinding leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.

The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is good, bad, usable, or unusable, so the design needs to be implemented and tested to determine whether it will work.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first.

A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and paper mockups of the look, feel, and functionality of an interface are a popular example.

Low-fidelity prototyping provides a quick and cheap way to make and modify prototypes compared with approaches that require coding and computers, and it is used primarily to brainstorm alternative designs and obtain user feedback on usability.

An interface sketch is a simple drawing that can be made on paper and depicts the major components of an interface, including the screen elements the user sees, buttons, selection options, their appearance, and their layout, so that an interface idea can be expressed to others or users for comments and feedback and its appearance can be envisioned.

To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

In a storyboard, each sketch is a keyframe, which is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time; the keyframes visualize the interaction for a specific task and its corresponding scenes, and the storyboard captures the sequence of user actions and the screen appearances the user sees from the beginning of the task to its end.
A medium-fidelity prototyping approach uses a computer to create simple prototypes without involving coding, whereas a low-fidelity prototyping approach does not rely on computers or digital media.
A high-fidelity prototyping approach uses computer programs or programming to create a prototype, so it is effectively actual software development, maybe on a reduced scale.

The prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation are at least a low-fidelity prototype, with higher-quality prototypes being better, and a team of evaluators.
Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

In a cognitive walkthrough, a scenario or task description is created for the evaluators, and the task described in the scenario is converted into interface-level tasks, which are the actions that must be performed in the prototype to accomplish that task; the evaluators then perform those actions with the prototype.

Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.
Nielsen's 10 heuristics is a general set of heuristics proposed in 1994 that is primarily related to graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but equally applicable to most interactive systems.

Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.

User evaluation is a quick evaluation technique that obtains feedback by asking users directly, and it requires user involvement, unlike expert evaluation techniques in which user involvement was optional.
In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions.

The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire consisting of three statements: 'I am satisfied with the ease of completing the tasks in this scenario'; 'I am satisfied with the amount of time it took to complete the tasks in this scenario'; and 'I am satisfied with the support information that is comprised of online help, messages, documentation when completing the tasks'.
The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire, containing statements rather than questions, that is administered at the end of a session after users have completed all the tasks.

In the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), users rate each statement on a seven-point rating scale in which rating 1 means strongly disagree with the statement and rating 7 means strongly agree with the statement.
The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire, containing statements rather than questions, that is administered at the end of a session after users have completed all the tasks.
Each System Usability Scale (SUS) statement is rated by the user on a 5-point agreement scale, where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree.

The System Usability Scale (SUS) score S is calculated from all 10 statement ratings r_i, with i from 1 to 10, as S = 2.5 × (Σ_{i∈{1,3,5,7,9}}(r_i − 1) + Σ_{i∈{2,4,6,8,10}}(5 − r_i)), where r_i is the user's rating for statement i.

Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, usability study, or empirical research, is a stage in interactive system development in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users.

Quick prototype evaluations are limited-scale early evaluations that use a limited number of evaluators and evaluate prototypes, so they can quickly identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about the overall usability of the end system.

A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

A testable research question, also called a hypothesis, is a question for which a study can be conducted to collect objective data, such as text entry speed, and draw objective conclusions independently of users' subjective interpretation.

A non-testable research question, also called an untestable question, is a question that cannot be directly tested objectively because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot be set up to collect objective data and, generally, a reliable scientific conclusion cannot be drawn.
A variable whose values are assigned and controlled is called an independent variable, also called a factor.
The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.

Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.

A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; in research question 3 (RQ3), the text entry rate (TER) is the dependent variable because its value depends on the interface, specifically the interface levels.
The empirical research process has four stages, the first stage being research question framing and the second stage being variables.

In the system implementation process, stage 4, data analysis, is the stage in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about the efficacy of a design, such as its text-entry speed.

A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds; using a homogeneous subset is acceptable when the system is for such a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group.

In experiment design, a user profile is a set of well-defined user profile characteristics or entries; the user is first defined by such a user profile, and experiment participants are selected only on the basis of that profile.

For an interface, a representative task set is a small, well-defined subset of tasks that are used by everybody most of the time, namely the tasks that potential users most frequently or commonly use when the interface is deployed in practice, and in an empirical study one or more tasks from this set should ideally be chosen so that the collected data and drawn conclusions are reliable.

In an experimental study, tasks can be assigned using a within-subject (repeated measures) design, in which every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions, or a between-subjects design, in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.

In a within-subject design, the practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice; it is also called a confounding variable and confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface.
A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant, for example by shifting a numbered task sequence one position for each successive participant.
